name: Grant Writing Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building grant writing — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary grant writing tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building grant writing — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary grant writing tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep grant writing outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
2. Check that grant writing terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
3. When multiple grant writing strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
4. When grant writing guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
5. Before starting grant writing work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
6. Surface known limitations of a chosen grant writing approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
7. Prefer explicit, readable grant writing solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic grant writing advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new grant writing abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not silently drop grant writing edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid mixing unrelated grant writing concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting grant writing assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for grant writing, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
